title: Distinct Orderings of a Multiset
statement:
You get an array nums that may contain repeated values. Return every different way to arrange all of its values in a row.

Two arrangements count as the same if they read the same value by value, so each one must appear exactly once in your answer. The arrangements may come in any order.

examples.why: Treating the two 2s as different gives 6 orderings, but they pair up into 3 that read the same.
With no repeats every ordering is distinct.
All values equal: only one row is possible.

hints: Plain permutation code creates the same row several times when values repeat. Can you avoid creating them instead of filtering afterwards?
At each position, you only care about which value goes there, not which copy of it. Try each distinct value once per position.
Count how many copies of each value are left. At each position loop over the values with a count above zero, use one, recurse, then give it back.

explain.intuition:
Duplicates appear because the search treats the two 2s in [2, 2, 5] as different items: "first 2 then second 2" and "second 2 then first 2" both produce [2, 2, …]. The fix is to decide per position which value goes there, never which copy.

A count map does that naturally. Keep how many of each value are still unused. To fill the next slot, loop over the distinct values that still have copies, take one, recurse, and put it back. Two branches at the same slot always place different values, so no row can be built twice, and no set of seen rows is needed. It is the same idea as a UI that groups identical items into "×3" instead of listing them separately.
steps: Recurse with a growing row. When it holds every value, save a copy.
Otherwise, for each distinct value whose count is above zero: decrease the count, push the value, recurse, pop it, restore the count.
pitfalls: Generating all orderings and deduplicating with a set. It works, but it does all the repeated work first and needs a way to hash rows.
With the sort-and-skip version, skipping a duplicate when the previous equal value is still unused gets flipped easily. The rule is: skip nums[i] if it equals nums[i−1] and nums[i−1] is not used yet.
Saving row itself instead of a copy, so every saved row ends up as the same emptied array.

complexity.time: O(n · n!) in the worst case

solutions.title: All orderings, then deduplicate
solutions.idea: Build every ordering of the positions and keep a set of the rows already produced.

solutions.title: Backtracking over value counts
solutions.idea: Pick a value, not a copy, for each slot. A count map makes repeated rows impossible.

solutions.title: Sort and skip equal neighbours
solutions.idea: Sort so equal values sit together. Use equal values strictly left to right: skip a copy while the one before it is still unused.

followups: Return only the k-th distinct ordering in sorted order, without listing the others.
How many distinct orderings are there? Give a formula from the value counts.
